questions.title: INNER JOIN vs. LEFT JOIN
questions.prompt: In SQL Server, what is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN? Specifically, what happens to rows that don't have a match on the other side in each case?
questions.modelAnswer: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the ON condition evaluates true on both sides — any row from either table that has no match on the other side is dropped from the result entirely. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in the FROM clause (the 'left' table), whether or not it has a match in the table named after JOIN (the 'right' table). When a left-table row has no match, every column that would have come from the right table comes back as NULL instead of the row being dropped. 'Left' and 'right' describe position in the query text — the table in FROM is left, the table after JOIN is right — not anything about the size or importance of the data. A common real use of LEFT JOIN is combining it with WHERE <right-table-column> IS NULL to find rows that have no match at all, since that column can only be NULL if the join failed to find a partner row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with a concrete example: if I join Product to SalesOrderDetail with an INNER JOIN, I only see products that have actually sold — a product sitting in inventory with zero orders just disappears from the result, because there's nothing on the right side to pair it with. If my actual question is 'show me every product, including the ones that have never sold,' INNER JOIN can't answer that by definition, so I switch to a LEFT JOIN from Product. Now every product shows up, and for the ones with no matching order, the order columns just come back NULL. That NULL is actually useful — if I add WHERE OrderQty IS NULL to that LEFT JOIN, I've just built a 'products that have never sold' report, which is a query I get asked for constantly in a reporting role. The one thing I'm careful to remember is that left and right only refer to where I physically wrote the table in the query, not which table is 'bigger' or more important.
questions.example:
-- INNER JOIN: only products with at least one order line
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- LEFT JOIN: every product, NULL-filled when there's no match
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- Finding products that have NEVER sold
SELECT p.Name
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID
WHERE sod.ProductID IS NULL;
commonMistakes: Thinking 'left' and 'right' describe which table has more rows or matters more, instead of just position in the FROM/JOIN clause
Forgetting that unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL, then getting confused when COUNT() or SUM() on those columns behaves unexpectedly
Using INNER JOIN when the real goal is to find rows with no match — that specifically requires LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL check
Not realizing WHERE runs after the join, so a WHERE clause on a right-side column can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN back into something that behaves like an INNER JOIN
keyPoints: INNER JOIN returns only rows matching on both sides
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in FROM, matched or not
Left/right refer to position in the query, not data meaning or size
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL in a LEFT JOIN
LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is the standard pattern for finding unmatched rows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what each join type returns
Explains NULL behavior for unmatched LEFT JOIN rows
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: WHERE vs. HAVING
questions.prompt: Why can't you filter on the result of an aggregate function (like AVG or COUNT) using a WHERE clause, and how does HAVING solve that problem? What is the correct logical order of FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, and ORDER BY?
questions.modelAnswer: WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY runs, so at the point WHERE executes, groups and their aggregated values (like AVG(ListPrice)) don't exist yet — there's nothing for WHERE to compare against. HAVING is WHERE's counterpart for groups: it runs after GROUP BY has formed the groups and after the aggregate functions have been computed, so by the time HAVING evaluates, every group's aggregate already exists and can be filtered on. The correct logical processing order in T-SQL is: FROM (and JOIN) first, then WHERE filters individual rows, then GROUP BY forms groups, then HAVING filters those groups, then SELECT picks the columns/expressions to return, and finally ORDER BY sorts the final result. WHERE and HAVING aren't mutually exclusive — you commonly use WHERE to remove rows before grouping even starts, and HAVING to filter the groups that result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as a timeline problem, not a syntax problem. If I write WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500, SQL Server throws an error, because logically WHERE runs before GROUP BY has even created any groups — there's no average to check yet. The moment I actually need to filter on an aggregated value, I move that condition to HAVING, which runs after the grouping and aggregation have already happened. In practice I use both together constantly: WHERE Color IS NOT NULL to throw out rows with no color recorded before I even start grouping, then GROUP BY Color, then HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500 to keep only the color groups whose average price clears that bar. I always come back to the same six-step order — FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY — whenever I'm unsure why a query is or isn't behaving the way I expect.
questions.example:
SELECT Color, AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
HAVING AVG(ListPrice) > 500;
-- WHERE removes NULL-color rows before grouping; HAVING keeps only
-- the color groups whose computed average price exceeds 500.
commonMistakes: Writing WHERE AVG(ListPrice) > 500 and being surprised by the error instead of recognizing aggregates aren't available yet at that stage
Assuming WHERE and HAVING are interchangeable, rather than realizing WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups
Not knowing the logical processing order, which makes debugging any non-trivial query much harder
Putting a filter that doesn't need aggregation into HAVING instead of WHERE, which is valid but wastes work filtering rows that could have been removed earlier
keyPoints: WHERE filters individual rows and runs before GROUP BY
HAVING filters groups and runs after GROUP BY and aggregation
Logical order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY
WHERE and HAVING can and often should be used together

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why WHERE can't reference aggregates
Correctly states the logical processing order
Explains how WHERE and HAVING work together

questions.title: Primary keys vs. foreign keys
questions.prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY constraint guarantee about a column, and what does a FOREIGN KEY constraint enforce between two tables? What happens if you try to insert a row that violates a foreign key?
questions.modelAnswer: A primary key guarantees two things at once about a column (or set of columns): every value is unique, and no value is ever NULL — together that means a primary key value always identifies exactly one row. Creating a primary key without specifying otherwise also builds a clustered index on it by default, physically sorting the table by that key. A foreign key enforces referential integrity: every value in the foreign-key column must already exist as a primary-key value in the referenced table. Trying to insert or update a row with a foreign-key value that doesn't exist in the referenced table fails with error 547 — the database physically refuses to create the orphaned row. ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default behavior (which blocks deleting a referenced row while dependents still point to it) so that deleting a parent row automatically deletes its dependent rows too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the primary key as the table's identity guarantee — Production.Product's primary key, ProductID, means I can always find exactly one product for a given ID, never zero, never two. The foreign key is what makes a JOIN trustworthy: Product.ProductSubcategoryID is a foreign key to ProductSubcategory, so SQL Server physically won't let me insert a product pointing at a subcategory that doesn't exist. If I try, I get error 547, which is the database doing its job, not a bug to work around. I'm careful with ON DELETE CASCADE, though — it's convenient for cleaning up dependent rows automatically, but on a deep relationship chain it can silently delete far more data than I expect, so I think through the blast radius before turning it on.
commonMistakes: Thinking a primary key only guarantees uniqueness and forgetting it also guarantees NOT NULL
Not realizing a primary key builds a clustered index by default unless you explicitly say NONCLUSTERED
Assuming a foreign key violation is just a warning rather than a hard failure (error 547) that blocks the write
Adding ON DELETE CASCADE without considering how far the deletion could cascade through a longer relationship chain
keyPoints: Primary key = unique + NOT NULL, identifying exactly one row
Primary key creates a clustered index by default
Foreign key enforces that a value must exist as a primary key in another table
Violating a foreign key raises Error 547
ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default block-on-delete behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a primary key guarantees
Correctly describes referential integrity and Error 547
Mentions the clustered index / cascade nuance

questions.title: CTEs vs. regular subqueries
questions.prompt: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE), and how does it differ from writing the same logic as a regular subquery? Why might you prefer a CTE?
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named, temporary result set defined at the top of a query with the WITH keyword. Functionally, it's equivalent to putting the same SELECT inside a subquery in the FROM clause — but instead of nesting it inline, you give it a name once and then reference that name like a real table in the statement that follows. This makes deeply nested subqueries much easier to read, especially when the same intermediate result needs to be referenced more than once in the outer query. A CTE is strictly temporary: it only exists for the single statement immediately following its WITH clause, is never saved anywhere, and disappears the moment that statement finishes — unlike a VIEW, which is a genuinely reusable, saved named query.
questions.professionalAnswer: I reach for a CTE mainly for readability. A subquery nested three levels deep inside a FROM clause gets hard to read fast — you end up mentally tracking which closing parenthesis belongs to which level. If I give that same logic a name with WITH CategoryAverages AS (...), I can read the outer query almost like English: 'from CategoryAverages, where...' That's especially valuable when I need to reference the same intermediate calculation more than once in the final query, since a CTE lets me do that without repeating the underlying SELECT. The one thing I always clarify for someone newer to this is that a CTE isn't a saved object — it only lives for the one statement right after it, so if I need that same logic reused across multiple separate queries, a VIEW is the right tool, not a CTE.
questions.example:
WITH CategoryAverages AS (
    SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, AVG(ListPrice) AS AvgPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID
)
SELECT ca1.ProductSubcategoryID, ca1.AvgPrice
FROM CategoryAverages AS ca1
WHERE ca1.AvgPrice > (SELECT AVG(AvgPrice) FROM CategoryAverages);
-- CategoryAverages is referenced twice in one statement -- hard to
-- do cleanly with a nested subquery instead.
commonMistakes: Thinking a CTE is saved/reusable across separate queries like a VIEW, rather than scoped to one statement
Not taking advantage of referencing the same CTE multiple times in the outer query
Assuming a CTE is always faster than a subquery -- it's primarily a readability tool, not automatically a performance one
Forgetting the WITH keyword needs to be the first word of the batch (or preceded by a semicolon) in some contexts
keyPoints: CTE = a named, temporary result set defined with WITH
Functionally equivalent to a FROM-clause subquery, but far more readable
Can be referenced multiple times in the statement that follows it
Scoped to one statement only -- not saved like a VIEW

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what a CTE is
Explains the readability/multiple-reference advantage
Correctly notes the CTE is scoped to one statement, unlike a VIEW

questions.title: UNION vs. UNION ALL
questions.prompt: In T-SQL, what's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL when combining the result sets of two SELECT statements, and what two conditions must both SELECT statements satisfy before you can combine them at all?
questions.modelAnswer: UNION combines the rows returned by two (or more) SELECT statements into one result set and removes any duplicate rows from that combined set, which requires SQL Server to do an implicit sort/distinct pass over the whole combined output. UNION ALL also combines the rows, but keeps every row exactly as returned, duplicates included, and skips the dedup pass entirely -- which makes it faster and cheaper to run whenever duplicates either can't occur or genuinely don't matter. Both statements being combined must return the same number of columns, and the data type in each corresponding column position must be compatible (not necessarily identical, but implicitly convertible) -- column names in the final result come from the first SELECT statement, regardless of what the second one used.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default to UNION ALL unless I actually have a reason to expect duplicates and need them removed, because UNION ALL skips the sort/distinct work UNION does under the hood, so it's just cheaper to run on anything beyond a trivial row count. The two things I always check before combining two SELECTs this way: same number of columns on both sides, and compatible data types lining up column-by-column -- if the second SELECT's third column is a different, incompatible type from the first's third column, the combine fails outright. One detail that trips people up is that the final column names come entirely from the first SELECT -- aliasing a column differently in the second query doesn't change anything in the output.
questions.example:
-- UNION: removes duplicate rows across both queries
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';

-- UNION ALL: keeps every row, including duplicates, and skips the dedup work
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION ALL
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';
commonMistakes: Using UNION by default everywhere, paying for a dedup pass that isn't actually needed
Assuming the two SELECTs need identical column names instead of just a matching column count and compatible types
Not realizing the final result's column names come from the first SELECT, regardless of aliases used in the second
Forgetting ORDER BY can only appear once, at the very end of the combined statement, not after each individual SELECT
keyPoints: UNION removes duplicate rows across the combined result sets; UNION ALL keeps every row
UNION ALL is cheaper -- it skips the sort/distinct pass UNION performs
Both SELECTs must return the same number of columns with compatible data types per position
Result column names come from the first SELECT statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the duplicate-removal difference
Correctly states the column-count/data-type compatibility requirement
Mentions the performance implication of the dedup pass

questions.title: What a DAG actually is
questions.prompt: What is a DAG in Airflow, and why does the 'acyclic' part of that name specifically matter?
questions.modelAnswer: DAG stands for Directed Acyclic Graph, and in Airflow it's the Python object that defines a pipeline: a collection of tasks, plus the dependencies between them, expressed as directed edges (task A must finish before task B starts). 'Directed' means each dependency has a direction -- A points to B, not the reverse -- which is what lets Airflow know the correct order to run tasks in. 'Acyclic' means the graph can never loop back on itself: there's no path that starts at a task and eventually leads back to that same task. This matters because a cycle (A depends on B, which depends on A) would have no valid starting point -- Airflow would have no way to decide which task to run first, since each one is waiting on the other. Airflow enforces this at DAG-parse time: if you accidentally define a circular dependency, the DAG fails to load at all rather than running and getting stuck, which surfaces the mistake immediately instead of silently deadlocking during a scheduled run.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd break the acronym down literally, since it actually describes the thing precisely. It's a graph -- tasks as nodes, dependencies as connections between them. It's directed -- each connection has an order, task A has to finish before task B starts, not the other way around. And it's acyclic -- no loop is allowed, so there's no scenario where task A is secretly waiting on task B which is secretly waiting on task A. That last part isn't a minor technicality -- if a cycle like that were allowed, Airflow would have no valid place to start, since every task in the loop is blocked on another task in the same loop. Airflow actually catches this for you: if you write a circular dependency by mistake, the DAG won't even load in the UI, which is a much better failure mode than a pipeline that silently hangs forever during a 2 AM run.
commonMistakes: Thinking DAG is just Airflow's name for 'a pipeline' without understanding what directed and acyclic specifically mean
Accidentally creating a circular dependency and not understanding why the DAG fails to even load
Assuming tasks in a DAG run in the order they're written in the file, rather than in the order their dependencies dictate
Confusing a DAG definition (the Python file) with a DAG run (one actual execution of that pipeline on a given schedule)
keyPoints: DAG = Directed Acyclic Graph: tasks as nodes, dependencies as directed edges
'Directed' establishes the required order between two tasks
'Acyclic' guarantees no circular dependency, so there's always a valid starting point
Airflow refuses to load a DAG with a circular dependency rather than letting it run and hang

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines DAG and its three components (graph, directed, acyclic)
Explains why a cycle would be unresolvable
Mentions Airflow's handling of an accidental cycle

questions.title: Delta Lake vs. plain Parquet
questions.prompt: What is Delta Lake, and what does it add on top of a plain Parquet table that a data engineer actually relies on day to day?
questions.modelAnswer: A plain Parquet table is just a folder of columnar data files with no record of its own history -- there's no transaction log, no guarantee that a write that's interrupted halfway through doesn't leave the table in a half-written, corrupted state, and no built-in way to see what the data looked like yesterday. Delta Lake is that same Parquet file format plus a transaction log (the _delta_log folder) sitting alongside it, which is what actually adds the useful guarantees: ACID transactions, so a write either fully commits or doesn't happen at all, even if two processes write at the same time; schema enforcement, so a write with an unexpected or mismatched schema is rejected rather than silently corrupting the table; and time travel, which uses the transaction log's history to query the table as it looked at an earlier version or point in time. None of that comes from Parquet alone -- Parquet is the storage format, Delta Lake is the layer of metadata and guarantees built on top of it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say Delta Lake isn't a replacement for Parquet, it's Parquet plus a transaction log. The actual data files underneath a Delta table are still Parquet files -- what Delta adds is the _delta_log folder next to them, which records every write as a transaction. That log is what gives me ACID guarantees, so two jobs writing to the same table at the same time don't corrupt it the way they could with plain Parquet; it's what enforces schema, so a job writing the wrong columns gets rejected instead of silently polluting the table; and it's what makes time travel possible, since I can ask Delta to show me the table as it looked three versions ago and it just replays the log. If I'm working with plain Parquet and none of that exists, I'm on my own for all three of those guarantees.
commonMistakes: Thinking Delta Lake is a completely different file format from Parquet, rather than Parquet plus a transaction log
Assuming a plain Parquet table gets the same ACID guarantees as Delta automatically
Not knowing time travel comes specifically from the transaction log's history, not from the data files themselves
Forgetting that concurrent writers to a plain Parquet table can genuinely corrupt it, which Delta's transaction log is built to prevent
keyPoints: Delta Lake = Parquet data files + a transaction log (_delta_log)
The transaction log provides ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel
Plain Parquet has none of those guarantees on its own
Concurrent writes to plain Parquet can corrupt the table; Delta's log prevents that

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what Delta Lake adds (transaction log, ACID, schema enforcement, time travel)
Correctly distinguishes Delta Lake from plain Parquet
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Spark transformations vs. actions
questions.prompt: In Spark, what's the difference between a transformation (like filter or select) and an action (like count or show), and why does Spark wait to actually run anything until an action is called?
questions.modelAnswer: A transformation (filter, select, withColumn, join, and similar) doesn't touch any data when it's called -- it just adds one more step to a logical plan Spark is building up in the background, describing what should eventually happen. An action (count, show, collect, write, and similar) is what actually triggers Spark to execute that whole accumulated plan against the real data and produce a concrete result. This is called lazy evaluation: Spark deliberately waits because it's more efficient to look at the entire chain of transformations at once and optimize it as a whole -- reordering filters, combining steps, deciding how to partition work -- than to execute each transformation immediately and separately as it's written. A practical consequence is that calling df.filter(...) alone does nothing observable at all; nothing actually runs until something like df.filter(...).count() reaches an action.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as the difference between writing a recipe and actually cooking. Every transformation I chain -- filter, select, withColumn -- just adds a line to the recipe; Spark doesn't touch any data yet, it's just building up a plan of what to do. The moment I call an action like count() or write(), Spark finally reads that whole recipe and executes it all at once, which lets it optimize the entire chain together rather than running each step the moment I write it. The thing that catches people off guard the first time is that if I write df.filter(col('Amount') > 100) on its own line and nothing happens, that's completely expected -- filter is a transformation, so Spark hasn't actually done anything yet. It's also why re-running count() on the same unchained DataFrame twice re-executes the whole plan from scratch, unless I've explicitly cached it.
commonMistakes: Expecting a transformation like filter() to immediately scan or change the data
Not realizing an error inside a transformation chain might not surface until an action is finally called
Calling an action repeatedly and being surprised the whole plan reruns each time instead of being remembered automatically
Confusing show() (an action that returns results) with a transformation, since it looks similar to printing a DataFrame
keyPoints: Transformations build a logical plan lazily; they don't touch data when called
Actions trigger Spark to actually execute the accumulated plan
Lazy evaluation lets Spark optimize the whole chain before running anything
Nothing observable happens until an action is reached; the plan re-executes each time an action is called unless cached

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes transformations from actions
Explains lazy evaluation and why Spark waits for an action
Gives correct examples of each

questions.title: Kafka topics, producers, and consumers at a glance
questions.prompt: At a basic level, what is a Kafka topic, and what roles do producers and consumers each play around it?
questions.modelAnswer: A Kafka topic is a named, durable, append-only log that records get written into and read from -- conceptually similar to a named feed or channel, split internally into partitions for parallelism. A producer is any application that writes (publishes) records into a topic; it has no knowledge of who, if anyone, is reading those records. A consumer is any application that reads (subscribes to) records from a topic, at its own pace, independently of when they were written. Critically, a topic doesn't behave like a traditional queue where a message disappears once someone reads it -- records stay in the topic for a configured retention period (time- or size-based) regardless of whether any consumer has read them yet, which means multiple independent consumers (or consumer groups) can each read the exact same records, at different times, without affecting each other or the producer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a topic as a durable, ordered log that things get appended to, not a mailbox that empties out as it's read. A producer's whole job is writing records into that log -- it doesn't know or care who's going to read them, or whether anyone's even listening yet. A consumer's job is reading records out of that log at its own pace, and because the records aren't deleted just because one consumer read them, a second, completely independent consumer can come along later and read the same data from the beginning if it needs to. That retention behavior is the part that surprises people coming from a traditional message queue mindset, where a message is gone the moment it's consumed -- in Kafka, the topic keeps holding onto records for as long as its retention policy says, so 'did anyone read this yet' isn't really a question that affects whether the data is still there.
commonMistakes: Assuming a message disappears from the topic once a consumer reads it, like a traditional queue
Not realizing a topic is physically split into partitions, which is part of how Kafka parallelizes reads and writes
Thinking a producer needs a consumer to be actively running at the same time for a write to succeed
Confusing 'topic' with a single file rather than a logical, partitioned, append-only log
keyPoints: A topic is a durable, partitioned, append-only log
Producers write records into a topic; consumers read from it independently
Records aren't removed from the topic just because a consumer read them -- they're retained per a configured policy
Multiple independent consumers can read the same topic without affecting each other or the producer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a topic as a durable, partitioned log
Correctly describes producer and consumer roles
Explains that messages aren't removed on read, unlike a traditional queue

questions.title: Unity Catalog, at a glance
questions.prompt: At a basic level, what problem does Unity Catalog in Databricks actually solve, and what's the simplest way to describe what it adds on top of a regular Databricks workspace?
questions.modelAnswer: Before Unity Catalog, permissions and metadata in Databricks were typically managed separately per workspace, which meant there was no single, consistent place to see who could access which table across an entire organization, and no built-in way to track where a table's data actually came from. Unity Catalog is a centralized governance layer sitting above the workspace level: it adds one place to manage access control (grants on catalogs, schemas, tables, and even rows/columns) and one place that automatically records data lineage -- which notebooks, jobs, or queries read from and wrote to a given table -- across every workspace attached to it, not just one. At the simplest level, think of it as the difference between every workspace keeping its own separate, disconnected list of 'who can see what,' versus one shared, organization-wide rulebook and audit trail that every workspace reads from and writes to.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the problem first: without Unity Catalog, permissions live at the workspace level, so if a company has five Databricks workspaces, there are potentially five separate, disconnected answers to 'who can see this table,' and no single place that actually shows where a table's data came from or who touched it. Unity Catalog fixes that by sitting above all those workspaces as one shared governance layer -- one place to grant or revoke access, and one place that automatically tracks lineage, regardless of which workspace a query happened to run in. If someone asks me to explain it simply, I'd say it turns 'every workspace manages its own rules' into 'one rulebook the whole organization shares,' which is exactly the kind of thing that matters a lot more once a company has more than one team and more than one workspace.
commonMistakes: Thinking Unity Catalog is just a naming convention rather than an actual centralized governance and permissions layer
Assuming permissions and lineage were already organization-wide before Unity Catalog, rather than workspace-scoped
Confusing Unity Catalog with the storage format (Delta) rather than the governance layer sitting on top of it
Not realizing lineage tracking is largely automatic, not something that has to be manually documented
keyPoints: Without Unity Catalog, permissions and metadata are typically scoped per workspace, with no shared view
Unity Catalog is a centralized governance layer spanning every attached workspace
It adds one shared place for access control and automatic data lineage tracking
It matters most once an organization has more than one workspace or team

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the problem Unity Catalog solves (fragmented, workspace-scoped governance)
Correctly describes what Unity Catalog adds (centralized access control and lineage)
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Write a GROUP BY aggregate query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns each distinct Color along with the count of products of that color and the average ListPrice for that color, excluding rows where Color is NULL.
questions.code:
-- Production.Product (AdventureWorks2012) has columns including:
-- ProductID, Name, Color, ListPrice
USE AdventureWorks2012;
GO
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY works in three conceptual steps: split the table into groups (one group per distinct Color value), aggregate within each group separately (COUNT and AVG each run once per group, not once overall), then combine the results into one row per group. Every column in SELECT must either be wrapped in an aggregate function or listed in GROUP BY — Color qualifies because it's the GROUP BY column; Name would not be allowed unaggregated here because it varies within a color group. Filtering out NULL colors belongs in WHERE, since that's a row-level filter that should happen before grouping, not a group-level filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write WHERE Color IS NOT NULL first, since that's just removing rows before grouping even starts — no reason to let NULL colors form their own group if the business doesn't care about them. Then GROUP BY Color splits the remaining rows into one bucket per color, and COUNT(*) plus AVG(ListPrice) each compute their own answer per bucket rather than one answer for the whole table. The result has exactly one row per distinct color — the same number of rows COUNT(DISTINCT Color) would report — which is a good sanity check I'd run after writing a query like this.
questions.example:
SELECT Color,
       COUNT(*) AS ProductCount,
       AVG(ListPrice) AS AveragePrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE Color IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Color
ORDER BY ProductCount DESC;
-- One row per distinct Color; COUNT and AVG are computed per color group.
commonMistakes: Adding Name or another non-aggregated, non-grouped column to SELECT and getting a GROUP BY error
Filtering NULL colors with HAVING instead of WHERE, doing unnecessary work by grouping rows that should have been excluded first
Forgetting WHERE Color IS NOT NULL entirely and getting an extra group for NULL
Confusing COUNT(*) (counts rows) with COUNT(Color) (counts non-NULL Color values) when NULLs are still present
keyPoints: GROUP BY splits rows into groups, aggregates within each, then combines into one row per group
Every SELECT column must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY
Row-level filters (like excluding NULL) belong in WHERE, before grouping
Result row count should match COUNT(DISTINCT <grouped column>)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct GROUP BY syntax and aggregate functions
Correctly excludes NULL colors with WHERE, not HAVING
Explains why the query is structured that way

questions.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK side by side
questions.prompt: Write a query that ranks products by ListPrice descending using ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in the same result set, and explain how the three functions differ when two products are tied for the same price.
questions.modelAnswer: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique, sequential numbers — even for genuinely tied values, it arbitrarily breaks the tie and gives one row a lower number than the other. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but leaves a gap afterward: if two products tie for rank 1, the next distinct price gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() accounts for how many rows were tied at the previous rank. DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but with no gap — the next distinct price after a tie at rank 1 gets rank 2. All three are computed with an OVER (ORDER BY ...) window clause and require no GROUP BY.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run all three in one query so the difference is visible directly in the output rather than just described. If two products are tied for the most expensive, ROW_NUMBER() pretends there's no tie at all and numbers them 1 and 2 arbitrarily — which would misrepresent a genuine tie as a win. RANK() is honest about the tie: both get rank 1, but the next product jumps to rank 3, because two rows already occupied rank 1's 'slot.' DENSE_RANK() is also honest about the tie — both get rank 1 — but it only cares about distinct values, so the next price tier is rank 2 with no gap. Which one I pick depends on the business question: a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for second place genuinely skips third place calls for RANK(); a scale of distinct price tiers where I just want the next gap-free tier number calls for DENSE_RANK().
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- Tied prices: RowNum stays unique, Rank_ ties then skips ahead,
-- DenseRank_ ties with no gap.
commonMistakes: Assuming ROW_NUMBER() is 'safer' for ties when it actually hides them by assigning arbitrary unique numbers
Confusing RANK's gap-after-a-tie behavior with DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Forgetting that ORDER BY inside OVER() determines which rows get which rank — changing it changes the whole result
Trying to use these functions without an OVER() clause, or expecting them to need a GROUP BY
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, even for ties
RANK() ties share a number but the next value skips ahead by the tie size
DENSE_RANK() ties share a number with no gap for the next distinct value
All three run inside OVER (ORDER BY ...), no GROUP BY needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct syntax for all three ranking functions
Accurately explains the tie-handling difference
Picks a sensible real-world scenario for each function

questions.title: Write a parameterized stored procedure
questions.prompt: Write a stored procedure named usp_GetProductsAbovePrice that accepts a @MinPrice parameter defaulting to 100, and returns the Name and ListPrice of every product in Production.Product with a ListPrice at or above that value, ordered by price descending. Then show how you'd call it both with and without supplying a value for @MinPrice.
questions.modelAnswer: A parameter is declared right after the procedure name, before the AS keyword, and behaves like a normal variable throughout the procedure body — it's just pre-populated from whatever the caller passes in. Giving a parameter a default value (@MinPrice MONEY = 100) makes it optional: if the caller doesn't supply a value, SQL Server uses the default automatically. Calling the procedure with named notation (EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500) is unambiguous and order-independent, which is why it's preferred over positional calling once a procedure has more than one parameter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the parameter with a sensible default so the procedure is usable both ways out of the box. The body itself is just the same filtered, sorted SELECT I'd write ad hoc, except @MinPrice stands in for whatever literal value I'd otherwise hard-code. Calling it with EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice; uses the default of 100 automatically, and calling it with @MinPrice = 500 overrides that for just this call. I always call with named parameters -- @MinPrice = 500 instead of just 500 -- because the moment a procedure picks up a second or third parameter, positional calling becomes an easy way to silently pass values to the wrong parameter.
questions.example:
CREATE PROCEDURE usp_GetProductsAbovePrice
    @MinPrice MONEY = 100
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT Name, ListPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    WHERE ListPrice >= @MinPrice
    ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
END;
GO

EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500; -- overrides the default
EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice;                 -- uses the default, 100
commonMistakes: Forgetting the default value, which forces every caller to always supply @MinPrice even when a sensible default exists
Calling the procedure positionally once it has multiple parameters, risking values landing in the wrong parameter
Putting the parameter declaration after AS instead of before it
Hard-coding the price threshold inside the procedure body instead of parameterizing it, defeating the point of a reusable procedure
keyPoints: Parameters are declared before AS and behave like pre-populated variables
A default value makes a parameter optional
Named notation (@Param = value) is unambiguous and order-independent
EXEC without a value for an optional parameter falls back to its default

Correct query logic (filter + sort)
Shows both calling styles (with and without override)

questions.title: Write a minimal two-task Airflow DAG
questions.prompt: Write a minimal Airflow DAG named daily_report_dag that runs once a day, with two PythonOperator tasks -- extract_data and load_data -- where load_data only runs after extract_data finishes successfully.
questions.code:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime

def extract():
    print("extracting...")

def load():
    print("loading...")
questions.modelAnswer: A DAG object is created with a unique dag_id, a schedule_interval (here, '@daily', a shorthand for running once every day), and a start_date, which anchors when the schedule begins. Each task is a PythonOperator instance with its own task_id and a python_callable pointing at the actual function to run. Dependencies between tasks are declared with the >> operator: extract_task >> load_task means extract_task must reach a successful completion state before load_task is even allowed to start; if extract_task fails, load_task is skipped by default rather than running against incomplete data. The DAG object itself doesn't run anything when the file is parsed -- it only defines the structure; the scheduler is what actually triggers individual task runs according to the schedule.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it close to the textbook minimum: a DAG with dag_id='daily_report_dag', schedule_interval='@daily', and a start_date, then two PythonOperator tasks, each pointing python_callable at my extract and load functions. The one line that actually encodes the dependency is extract_task >> load_task -- that's Airflow's shorthand for 'load_task can't start until extract_task has finished successfully.' If I got the order backwards and wrote load_task >> extract_task, I'd be telling Airflow to load before extracting, which is exactly the kind of mistake that's easy to make and easy to miss just by skimming the code, so I always read dependency lines left to right out loud to double check them.
questions.example:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime

def extract():
    print("extracting...")

def load():
    print("loading...")

with DAG(
    dag_id="daily_report_dag",
    schedule_interval="@daily",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
) as dag:
    extract_task = PythonOperator(task_id="extract_data", python_callable=extract)
    load_task = PythonOperator(task_id="load_data", python_callable=load)

    extract_task >> load_task
commonMistakes: Writing the dependency operator backwards (load_task >> extract_task), reversing the intended order
Forgetting start_date, without which the DAG has no anchor point for its schedule
Assuming the DAG file running top-to-bottom at parse time actually executes the tasks, rather than just defining the DAG's structure
Not setting catchup=False when a backfill of every missed schedule since start_date isn't actually wanted
keyPoints: A DAG needs a dag_id, schedule_interval, and start_date
Each task is an operator instance (PythonOperator here) with its own task_id and callable
>> declares a dependency: the left task must succeed before the right task starts
Parsing the DAG file defines its structure; the scheduler is what actually triggers runs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct DAG definition with required arguments
Correct PythonOperator task definitions
Correct dependency direction using >>

questions.title: Read a CSV into a DataFrame and filter it
questions.prompt: Write PySpark code that reads a CSV file located at '/mnt/raw/orders.csv' (with a header row) into a DataFrame, then returns only the rows where the Amount column is greater than 100.
questions.code:
# spark is an existing SparkSession
# File: /mnt/raw/orders.csv, has a header row, includes a numeric Amount column
questions.modelAnswer: Reading a CSV correctly requires two options: header, so the first row is treated as column names instead of data, and inferSchema, so numeric columns like Amount are read as actual numbers rather than strings (without it, every column defaults to string, and a numeric comparison like > 100 either fails or compares lexically instead of numerically). filter() is a transformation — it builds a step in the logical plan but doesn't execute anything on its own; an action like show() or count() is what actually triggers Spark to read the file and apply the filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd read it as spark.read.option('header', 'true').option('inferSchema', 'true').csv('/mnt/raw/orders.csv'), then filter with df.filter(col('Amount') > 100). The two options matter more than they look: without header, Spark treats the column names themselves as a data row; without inferSchema, Amount comes in as a string, and depending on the Spark version that numeric-looking comparison either throws an error or silently does a string comparison that doesn't mean what I want. I'd remember that filter() alone doesn't do anything observable — I'd need to call something like .show() or .count() afterward to actually see the filtered rows, since Spark doesn't read or process the file until an action forces it to.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

df = (
    spark.read
    .option("header", "true")
    .option("inferSchema", "true")
    .csv("/mnt/raw/orders.csv")
)

high_value_orders = df.filter(col("Amount") > 100)
high_value_orders.show()
commonMistakes: Forgetting the header option, which causes the header row itself to be read as a data row
Forgetting inferSchema, leaving every column as a string and breaking a numeric comparison
Calling filter() and expecting to see results immediately, without an action like show() or count()
Comparing Amount to the string "100" instead of the integer 100 once the column is correctly typed as numeric
keyPoints: spark.read needs header and inferSchema options set correctly for a CSV with a numeric column
filter() takes a Column expression, usually built with col()
filter() is lazy — nothing executes until an action like show() or count() is called
Without inferSchema, numeric comparisons on a CSV-sourced column can behave incorrectly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct read syntax with header/schema options
Correct filter syntax and logic
Explains the lazy evaluation implication

questions.title: Create a Delta table and query it
questions.prompt: Write the PySpark code to create a managed Delta table named sales_bronze from an existing DataFrame called raw_df, and then write a query that counts how many rows the table currently has.
questions.code:
# raw_df is an existing DataFrame with the data to load
# Goal: create a managed Delta table called sales_bronze, then count its rows
questions.modelAnswer: Writing raw_df.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('sales_bronze') does two things at once: it writes the underlying data as Delta-formatted Parquet files plus a transaction log, and it registers that table in the metastore under the name sales_bronze so it can be queried by name afterward, rather than just by file path. The mode argument matters — overwrite replaces the table's entire contents, while append adds to what's already there, and picking the wrong one either destroys existing data or silently duplicates it. Once the table exists, SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_bronze (or spark.table('sales_bronze').count() from PySpark) triggers an action that actually reads the table and returns its current row count.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write raw_df.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('sales_bronze') for the first run of this table. Being explicit about format('delta') matters to me even though it's often the default in a Databricks workspace, because I don't want the table's format depending on an environment default that could differ somewhere else. The mode is the detail I'd double check before running this against anything real — overwrite is right for a fresh load, but if this script runs again tomorrow and I actually meant to add that day's new rows, overwrite would wipe out everything already loaded, so I'd switch to append once this becomes a recurring job. Once the table's there, SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_bronze is the simplest sanity check that the write actually landed the number of rows I expected.
questions.example:
raw_df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("sales_bronze")

# Confirm the row count
spark.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS RowCount FROM sales_bronze").show()
# or: spark.table("sales_bronze").count()
commonMistakes: Using mode('overwrite') on a recurring job when append was actually intended, silently destroying previously loaded data
Using .save() with a file path instead of .saveAsTable(), which writes the files but doesn't register a queryable table name
Assuming format('delta') is unnecessary without checking what the workspace's actual default write format is
Forgetting that counting rows is an action — it actually reads the table rather than just describing it
keyPoints: .write.format('delta').mode(...).saveAsTable(...) creates a managed Delta table registered in the metastore
mode('overwrite') replaces all data; mode('append') adds to existing data
saveAsTable registers a queryable name; .save() to a path alone does not
COUNT(*) or .count() is an action that actually reads the table

Correct query to count rows

questions.title: Write a Terraform resource block
questions.prompt: Write a minimal Terraform resource block that provisions an Azure Storage Account named using a variable, in a given resource group and location, with Standard LRS replication.
questions.code:
# Goal: an azurerm_storage_account resource using var.storage_account_name,
# var.resource_group_name, and var.location, Standard tier, LRS replication
questions.modelAnswer: A Terraform resource block follows the shape resource "<resource_type>" "<local_name>" { ... } — the resource_type (azurerm_storage_account) tells Terraform which provider and which kind of object to create, and the local_name is just how this block is referred to elsewhere within the Terraform configuration, not the actual name Azure will show. The actual Azure-visible name is set inside the block with the name argument. account_tier and account_replication_type together control the storage redundancy — Standard and LRS here mean standard performance with locally redundant storage. Running terraform plan shows what Terraform would create or change without doing it, and terraform apply actually provisions the resource.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as resource "azurerm_storage_account" "raw_storage" { ... }, and the one thing I'd flag for someone newer to Terraform is that "raw_storage" there is purely a local reference I use elsewhere in this same configuration — it's not what shows up in the Azure portal. The name that actually matters in Azure is the name argument inside the block, which I'd drive from a variable so this block can be reused across environments without hardcoding anything. Before I'd ever apply this, I'd run terraform plan first to see exactly what Terraform intends to create, since plan costs nothing and catches a surprising number of mistakes before they touch real infrastructure.

resource "azurerm_storage_account" "raw_storage" {
  name                     = var.storage_account_name
  resource_group_name      = var.resource_group_name
  location                 = var.location
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"
}

Hardcoding values instead of using variables, making the block non-reusable across environments
Skipping terraform plan and going straight to apply without reviewing what will actually be created
Forgetting terraform init is needed before plan/apply will work against a given provider

// Goal: a 'location' param defaulting to resourceGroup().location,
// used by a Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts resource

I also keep in mind that what I'm writing isn't deployed as-is — the tooling compiles this Bicep file into an ARM JSON template first, and Bicep exists specifically to make writing and reading that ARM template less painful.

questions.title: Write a minimal Kafka producer
questions.prompt: Write a minimal Python Kafka producer that sends one JSON-encoded message, {'order_id': 1, 'amount': 42.50}, to a topic named 'orders'.
questions.code: # Goal: a KafkaProducer that sends one JSON message to the 'orders' topic
questions.modelAnswer: Kafka's wire protocol only transmits bytes, so a Python dict has to be explicitly serialized before it can be sent — passing value_serializer=lambda v: json.dumps(v).encode('utf-8') when constructing the KafkaProducer means every call to producer.send() automatically converts the value through that function first. producer.send('orders', value={...}) is asynchronous — it returns a future immediately rather than blocking until the message is actually delivered, so calling flush() (or close(), which flushes internally) afterward is what guarantees the message is actually sent to the broker before the script moves on or exits, rather than being silently lost if the process ends too soon.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd construct the producer with bootstrap_servers pointing at the cluster and a value_serializer that does json.dumps(...).encode('utf-8'), since Kafka only moves bytes around and a raw Python dict isn't bytes. Calling producer.send('orders', value={'order_id': 1, 'amount': 42.50}) kicks off the send, but it returns right away with a future rather than waiting for confirmation, so if my script just sent that and exited immediately, there's a real risk the message never actually made it to the broker before the process closed. I always call producer.flush() right after sending in a short script like this, specifically to force it to wait until the send is actually confirmed before moving on.
questions.example:
import json
from kafka import KafkaProducer

producer = KafkaProducer(
    bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092",
    value_serializer=lambda v: json.dumps(v).encode("utf-8"),
)

producer.send("orders", value={"order_id": 1, "amount": 42.50})
producer.flush()
commonMistakes: Passing a raw Python dict without a serializer, since Kafka clients only send bytes
Forgetting to call flush() or close(), risking the message never actually being sent before the script exits
Assuming producer.send() blocks until delivery is confirmed, when it actually returns a future immediately
Hardcoding the topic name with a typo that silently creates or targets a different topic than intended
keyPoints: KafkaProducer needs bootstrap_servers and a serializer for non-byte values
send() is asynchronous and returns a future immediately, not a confirmed result
flush()/close() ensures the message is actually delivered before the program continues or exits
Values must be serialized to bytes since Kafka's protocol only transmits bytes

questions.title: A minimal Auto Loader read
questions.prompt: At a basic level, what problem does Databricks Auto Loader solve compared to writing your own code to track which files in a folder have already been loaded, and what would the simplest possible Auto Loader read of a folder of CSV files look like?
questions.code:
# Goal: stream new CSV files landing in '/mnt/raw/orders/' into a DataFrame
# using Auto Loader (cloudFiles), without hand-tracking which files were already read
questions.modelAnswer: Without Auto Loader, incrementally loading only the new files in a folder means writing and maintaining your own bookkeeping -- a table or file tracking which filenames have already been processed, with logic to compare that list against what's currently in the folder every run. Auto Loader removes that bookkeeping entirely: it's a structured streaming source (format('cloudFiles')) that automatically keeps track, in its own checkpoint, of exactly which files it has already ingested, so each run (or continuous stream) only picks up files it hasn't seen before. The minimal setup needs cloudFiles.format (the file type being read, 'csv' here) and a checkpointLocation, which is where Auto Loader persists its own record of progress -- without that checkpoint path, it has nowhere to remember what it already loaded.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as Auto Loader doing the bookkeeping I'd otherwise have to build myself. Without it, I'd need some table tracking which filenames I've already pulled in, plus logic every run to diff that against what's actually sitting in the folder now -- that's real code to write and maintain just to avoid reprocessing the same files. With Auto Loader, I just point spark.readStream.format('cloudFiles') at the folder, tell it the file format, and give it a checkpointLocation, and it handles remembering what it's already seen on its own. The checkpoint path is the detail I'd never skip -- without it, Auto Loader has no memory between runs and would just reprocess everything from scratch every time.
questions.example:
df = (
    spark.readStream
    .format("cloudFiles")
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv")
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/mnt/raw/orders/_schema")
    .load("/mnt/raw/orders/")
)

(
    df.writeStream
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/raw/orders/_checkpoint")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)
    .toTable("orders_bronze")
)

Trying to hand-write file-tracking logic instead of letting cloudFiles handle it
Not setting cloudFiles.format to match the actual file type being read
Treating this as a one-time batch read instead of recognizing it's a structured streaming source, even when triggered to run once with availableNow

It's accessed through format('cloudFiles') as a structured streaming source

cloudFiles.format tells it what file type to expect in the folder

questions.title: Debugging a WHERE = NULL mistake
questions.prompt: A junior developer writes WHERE MiddleName = NULL to find customers with no middle name recorded, and gets zero rows back — even though many customers genuinely have a NULL MiddleName. What's actually wrong with that query, and how should they fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents an unknown or not-applicable value, not zero or an empty string. Because it's unknown, NULL can't be said to equal anything — not even another NULL — so any comparison using the = operator against NULL evaluates to unknown (treated as false), never true. That means WHERE MiddleName = NULL will always return zero rows, regardless of how many rows actually have a NULL MiddleName, because the comparison can never succeed. The fix is to use the special IS NULL syntax instead: WHERE MiddleName IS NULL. IS NULL isn't a comparison operator — it's dedicated syntax built specifically to test for the absence of a value, and it works correctly where = cannot. The same logic applies to IS NOT NULL for the opposite case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out is that this isn't a typo or syntax error — the query runs fine, it just silently returns the wrong answer, which is the dangerous kind of bug. I'd explain that NULL means 'unknown,' and you can't compare an unknown value to anything using = and expect a meaningful true or false — SQL Server treats that comparison as unknown, which gets filtered out just like false. So WHERE MiddleName = NULL isn't matching NULLs, it's failing to match anything at all. The fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, which is purpose-built syntax for exactly this case rather than a regular comparison. If the goal were actually to display something readable instead of filtering, I'd reach for ISNULL(MiddleName, '(none)') or COALESCE for more than two fallback values.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the query runs without error and silently returns the wrong result, rather than throwing an obvious failure
Treating NULL as if it were an empty string or zero instead of 'unknown'
Using = NULL or <> NULL anywhere instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Confusing ISNULL() (replaces a NULL with a default, two arguments) with IS NULL (tests for NULL)
keyPoints: NULL means unknown/not applicable, not zero or empty string
= NULL always evaluates to unknown/false, never true
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL is the only correct way to test for NULL
ISNULL()/COALESCE() substitute a default value rather than test for NULL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why = NULL fails silently
Provides the correct fix (IS NULL)
Mentions ISNULL/COALESCE as a related but different tool

questions.title: Diagnosing an accidental Cartesian product
questions.prompt: A query joining a 500-row Products table to a 100,000-row OrderDetail table unexpectedly returns 50 million rows instead of something in the few-hundred-thousand range. What almost certainly went wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: 50 million is exactly 500 times 100,000 -- the row-count signature of a Cartesian product, where every row of one table gets paired with every row of the other instead of only matching rows being paired. The most common real-world cause isn't a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- it's a missing or ineffective ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join: either the ON clause is left out entirely (old-style comma join with no join condition), or it exists but evaluates to true for nearly every row combination (for example ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which doesn't actually relate the two tables). To confirm it, check the join's ON clause first for a missing or non-relating condition, and as a general habit, sanity-check the row count after any join: if two tables of roughly 500 and 100,000 rows produce millions of result rows instead of a number in that rough range, that's an immediate signal to re-check the ON clause rather than assume the data is simply that large.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd notice is that 50 million is suspiciously close to 500 times 100,000 -- that's the fingerprint of a Cartesian product, not a coincidence. My first move is to go straight to the ON clause of the join and check two things: is it missing entirely, which happens with old comma-style joins that have no join condition at all, or does it exist but not actually relate the two tables -- something like ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which is true for almost every row and produces a Cartesian product in disguise even though there's technically an ON clause sitting there. Once I fix the condition to something that actually ties the tables together, like p.ProductID = sod.ProductID, I'd re-run the query and expect the row count to land in the same rough range as the bigger of the two tables, not multiply them together. I've made this a habit on every join I write now: sanity-check the row count before trusting the result.
questions.example:
-- BUG: no join condition at all -- a Cartesian product
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p, Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod;

-- BUG: ON clause exists but doesn't relate the tables
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.Name IS NOT NULL;

-- FIXED: a real join condition tying the tables together
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is just 'that big' instead of suspecting the join condition first
Not recognizing that an ON clause can exist and still produce a Cartesian product if it doesn't genuinely relate the tables
Never sanity-checking row counts after writing a join, so the problem isn't caught until it hits production
Confusing this with a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- the accidental version almost always comes from a broken or missing ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
keyPoints: Row count multiplying (500 x 100,000) instead of adding is the signature of a Cartesian product
Most accidental Cartesian products come from a missing or non-relating ON clause
Old-style comma joins with no ON clause default to a Cartesian product
An ON clause that's technically present but true for nearly every row is just as dangerous as none at all
Sanity-check row counts after any join as a standing habit

Correctly identifies missing/ineffective ON clause as the cause
