questions.title: SUM inflated after joining a one-to-many table
questions.prompt: A query joins SalesOrderHeader to SalesOrderDetail and correctly totals each order with SUM(LineTotal). After adding a third join to a Promotion table -- where some orders have more than one matching promotion row -- the total for those specific orders suddenly doubles or triples, even though nothing about the actual sales changed. The join conditions are all correct and genuinely relate the tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a Cartesian product -- every join condition is correct and genuinely relates the tables -- it's join fan-out, which happens whenever a correct join still has a one-to-many relationship on one side. Each SalesOrderDetail row that matches more than one Promotion row gets physically duplicated once per matching promotion before SUM ever runs, so SUM(LineTotal) is now adding the same line total two or three times for any order whose promotion happens to match more than once, while orders with exactly one (or zero) matching promotions are unaffected. The fix is to never combine two separate one-to-many expansions in a single flat join and then aggregate at the end -- instead, pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the grain actually needed, in its own subquery or CTE, before joining. Here, that means computing the order total from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail alone first, and only joining Promotion afterward (or in a separate query) if promotion details are genuinely needed, rather than letting its fan-out multiply rows that feed directly into the order-total SUM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that this isn't the Cartesian-product bug people usually learn about -- every join condition here is correct and really does relate the tables. This is fan-out: joining in a table that can legitimately match more than one row per order duplicates the order-detail rows underneath it, once per matching promotion, before the SUM even runs. So an order with two matching promotions gets its LineTotal counted twice, not because the math is wrong, but because the row genuinely got duplicated first. My fix is to separate the two aggregations: compute each order's total from just SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail in a CTE first, completely isolated from the Promotion join, and only bring Promotion into a separate query (or join it after the order total is already locked in) if I actually need promotion-level detail. The rule I'd apply going forward is never to let two independent one-to-many joins sit in the same flat query feeding one aggregate -- pre-aggregate each one to the grain I need first.
questions.example:
-- WRONG: Promotion's fan-out inflates the order total
SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
JOIN Sales.SpecialOfferProduct promo ON promo.ProductID = sod.ProductID
GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID;

-- FIXED: order total computed in isolation, before any promotion join
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
    JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
    GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID
)
SELECT * FROM OrderTotals;
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct, relating join condition rules out row duplication entirely
Not comparing row counts (or a known-good total) before and after adding the third join
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT ...) as a quick fix, which only coincidentally works and breaks again as soon as two genuinely different line totals happen to match
Combining two separate one-to-many expansions in one flat query feeding a single aggregate, instead of pre-aggregating each one to the grain actually needed
keyPoints: A correct join condition can still fan out rows when the relationship is genuinely one-to-many
Fan-out duplicates rows before aggregation runs, inflating any SUM downstream
This is distinct from a Cartesian product, which comes from a missing or non-relating join condition
Fix: pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the needed grain in its own subquery/CTE before joining further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fan-out (not a Cartesian product)
Explains why the duplication inflates the SUM
Proposes a correct fix (pre-aggregating before joining further)

questions.title: A new DAG isn't showing up in the Airflow UI at all
questions.prompt: You save a new DAG file into the dags folder, but after waiting several minutes, it never appears in the Airflow UI at all -- not even as a broken DAG. Where do you look, and what's the most likely cause?
questions.modelAnswer: The Airflow scheduler periodically scans the dags folder and tries to parse (import) every Python file it finds there -- 'tries to parse,' not 'successfully loads,' is the key distinction. If a DAG file has a Python syntax error or raises an exception at import time (a typo, a missing import, an indentation error), the scheduler fails to parse that file entirely and it never becomes a DAG object the UI can display -- which is why it doesn't even show up as a broken/red DAG, it simply doesn't exist from the UI's point of view. The place to look is the Airflow UI's own 'DAG Import Errors' panel (usually shown at the top of the DAGs list, or under Browse), which surfaces the exact Python exception and traceback for any file the scheduler couldn't import -- that's almost always faster and more direct than digging through raw scheduler logs. The fix is reading that traceback and correcting the actual Python error in the file; once it imports cleanly, the DAG appears in the UI on the next scheduler scan.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first stop is the DAG Import Errors panel right in the Airflow UI, not the scheduler logs, because that's specifically built to surface exactly this situation -- a file in the dags folder that the scheduler tried to import and couldn't. A DAG that never appears at all, not even broken, almost always means a Python-level problem in the file itself: a typo, a bad import, an indentation mistake -- something that throws an exception before Airflow ever gets to the point of registering it as a DAG object. The import errors panel shows me the actual traceback, which is usually enough to point straight at the broken line. Once I fix that specific error and save the file again, I just wait for the next scheduler scan and it shows up normally -- there's no restart or redeploy needed for a simple syntax fix like that in most setups.
commonMistakes: Assuming a missing DAG means a configuration problem instead of checking for a Python import error first
Digging through full scheduler logs before checking the dedicated DAG Import Errors panel, which surfaces this directly
Not realizing a DAG with an import-time exception won't appear even as a 'broken' DAG -- it simply won't exist in the UI at all
Assuming a fix requires restarting the scheduler, when the next automatic folder scan picks up a corrected file
keyPoints: The scheduler periodically scans and tries to import every file in the dags folder
A Python exception at import time means the DAG never gets registered -- it won't appear even as broken
The DAG Import Errors panel in the UI shows the exact traceback for any file that failed to import
Fixing the Python error and waiting for the next scan is usually all that's needed, no restart required

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies a Python import-time error as the likely cause
Correctly names the DAG Import Errors panel as where to look
Describes the correct resolution path

questions.title: A task is stuck in 'queued' and never starts running
questions.prompt: A DAG is scheduled correctly and shows up fine in the Airflow UI, but when it triggers, its tasks sit in a 'queued' state indefinitely and never move to 'running.' What are the most likely causes, and what would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Queued' means Airflow has decided a task is ready to run and has handed it off to be executed, but no actual worker process has picked it up yet -- the DAG and scheduling logic are working correctly; the problem is downstream, in execution capacity. The most common cause is that the executor (Celery, Kubernetes, or similar, depending on the setup) simply doesn't have any available worker to run the task -- either no worker process is running at all, or every available worker slot is already occupied by other tasks. A second common cause is a pool or concurrency limit -- Airflow lets you cap how many tasks can run simultaneously (globally, per-DAG, or via a named pool), and a task stuck in queued can simply be waiting for a slot that's fully occupied by other tasks. The first checks: confirm the worker process is actually running and reachable (not crashed or never started), and check whether a concurrency or pool limit is currently maxed out by other running tasks.
questions.professionalAnswer: 'Queued' tells me something specific: Airflow's scheduler has already decided this task is ready to go, so the DAG logic and scheduling aren't the problem here -- the problem is that nothing has actually picked the task up to run it yet. My first check is whether a worker is even running -- if the worker process crashed or was never started, tasks will queue forever with nothing wrong on the DAG side at all. If a worker is running, my next check is concurrency limits -- Airflow lets you cap how many tasks run at once, globally or through a named pool, and if every slot is already taken by other tasks, a newly queued task just waits its turn. I'd check both of those before assuming anything is actually wrong with the DAG itself, since a correctly-defined DAG stuck in queued is almost always an infrastructure/capacity issue, not a DAG-authoring one.
commonMistakes: Assuming a stuck-in-queued task means something is wrong with the DAG's own logic, rather than execution capacity
Not checking whether the worker process is actually running at all
Forgetting that concurrency or pool limits can hold a correctly-scheduled task in queued indefinitely
Restarting or rewriting the DAG before checking whether the issue is actually infrastructure-level
keyPoints: 'Queued' means the scheduler has approved the task but no worker has picked it up yet -- scheduling itself isn't the problem
Check first whether a worker process is actually running and reachable
Check concurrency/pool limits, which can hold a valid task in queued if all slots are occupied
A correctly-defined DAG stuck in queued usually points to infrastructure/capacity, not DAG authoring

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what 'queued' actually means
Correctly identifies worker availability as a likely cause
Correctly identifies concurrency/pool limits as a likely cause

questions.title: A Delta write fails with a schema mismatch error
questions.prompt: You run a daily append job writing a DataFrame into an existing Delta table, and it suddenly fails with a schema mismatch error after the source added a new column. What's happening, and what are your two realistic options to fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Delta enforces schema by default: an append whose DataFrame schema doesn't exactly match the target table's schema is rejected rather than silently written, which is schema enforcement protecting the table from accidental corruption. There are two realistic options. First, if the new column is actually wanted in the table going forward, intentionally allow it in with schema evolution — adding .option('mergeSchema', 'true') on the write (or enabling spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled) adds the new column to the table's schema, backfilling NULL for every row written before that column existed. Second, if the new column wasn't actually wanted in this table yet, select only the originally expected columns out of the DataFrame before writing, keeping the table's schema stable and letting the write succeed unchanged. Which option is right depends entirely on whether the new column should actually become part of the table now.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd first confirm this is schema enforcement doing its job, not a bug -- Delta deliberately rejects a write whose schema doesn't match rather than silently writing a half-matching row. Then it comes down to one question: do I actually want this new column in the table right now? If yes, I'd add mergeSchema as true on the write, which performs schema evolution -- it adds the column going forward and backfills NULL for every historical row, which I'd want the team to know about so nobody's surprised by NULLs appearing in older data. If the column isn't ready to be part of this table yet, I'd just select the DataFrame down to the columns the table already expects before writing, which keeps the schema stable and lets the job succeed without silently picking up something nobody's reviewed.
questions.example:
# Option 1: intentionally evolve the schema
raw_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("sales_bronze")

# Option 2: keep the existing schema, drop the new column for now
raw_df.select("OrderId", "Amount", "OrderDate").write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("sales_bronze")
commonMistakes: Assuming a schema mismatch error is a bug in Delta rather than deliberate schema enforcement
Turning on mergeSchema everywhere as a default habit instead of deciding deliberately whether the new column belongs in the table
Not realizing older rows get backfilled with NULL for a newly added column after schema evolution
Trying to force the write through without addressing the schema difference at all, rather than choosing one of the two real options
keyPoints: Schema enforcement blocks a mismatched write by default to protect the table
mergeSchema enables intentional schema evolution, adding the new column going forward
The alternative is trimming the DataFrame back to the existing schema before writing
Schema evolution backfills NULL for historical rows under the newly added column

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses schema enforcement as the cause
Describes the mergeSchema/schema evolution option
Describes the alternative of trimming the DataFrame to the existing schema

questions.title: Terraform apply fails saying a resource already exists
questions.prompt: You run terraform apply to provision a storage account that a teammate already created manually in the Azure portal, and it fails saying the resource already exists. Terraform's configuration is correct. What's the real problem, and how do you fix it without just deleting the existing resource?
questions.modelAnswer: Terraform's state file is its own record of what it believes it manages; a resource that exists in Azure but was never created through Terraform isn't in that state file, so Terraform has no way to know it already exists and tries to create a duplicate, which Azure rejects since the name must be unique. The fix (without deleting anything) is terraform import, which tells Terraform 'this resource already exists at this address, start tracking it in state without creating it' -- after import, a subsequent plan should show no changes if the configuration matches the real resource's settings exactly, or a diff if they don't match, which then needs reconciling.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real issue isn't the configuration — it's that Terraform's state file has no idea this resource exists, because it was created by hand instead of through Terraform. Terraform only ever knows about what's recorded in its own state, not everything that's actually sitting in the subscription, so it tries to create a new one and Azure rejects it as a duplicate name. Rather than deleting the manually-created resource and losing whatever's already configured on it, I'd run terraform import to attach that existing resource to the matching address in my configuration, which starts tracking it in state without touching it. After that, I'd run plan again — if my configuration doesn't exactly match the real resource's settings, plan will show a diff I still need to reconcile, so import isn't quite the end of the story by itself.
commonMistakes: Deleting the manually-created resource just to let Terraform create a fresh one, losing any data/config already on it
Not realizing Terraform's state file, not the configuration, is what tracks what Terraform believes exists
Forgetting that after import, the configuration still needs to match the real resource's actual settings or the next plan will show an unwanted diff
Assuming the 'already exists' error means the configuration itself is wrong, rather than a state-tracking gap
keyPoints: Terraform only knows about what's in its state file, not everything that exists in the cloud
terraform import links an existing resource to a config address without recreating it
Verify with plan afterward that the configuration matches reality
Deleting a manually-created resource to avoid this is risky and unnecessary

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the state-file gap as the cause
Proposes terraform import as the fix
Notes the need to verify configuration matches after import

questions.title: A Kafka consumer isn't receiving any messages
questions.prompt: A producer is confirmed to be successfully sending messages to a topic, but a new consumer application subscribed to that same topic isn't receiving anything at all. What are the most likely causes, and what would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common beginner cause is that the consumer's auto.offset.reset is set to 'latest' (often the default), meaning a brand-new consumer group only sees messages produced after it first connects -- if all the existing messages were produced before the consumer started, and nothing new has been sent since, the consumer genuinely has nothing new to read, which isn't a bug. The first check is whether this consumer belongs to a consumer group that already has committed offsets sitting at the end of the topic from an earlier run -- if so, it resumes from there, not from the beginning. A second common cause is a topic name typo or subscribing to the wrong topic entirely, since topic names are an exact, case-sensitive match. The fix is setting auto.offset.reset to 'earliest' if historical messages genuinely need to be read, or producing a fresh message once the consumer is confirmed running to test the pipeline end to end, along with double-checking the topic name matches exactly.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first check is auto.offset.reset, because 'latest' — which is a common default — means a brand-new consumer only sees messages produced from the moment it connects onward, not anything already sitting in the topic. If the producer sent its messages before this consumer ever started and nothing new has gone out since, there's genuinely nothing for it to read yet, and that's working as designed, not a bug. I'd also check whether this consumer group has run before and already has committed offsets at the end of the topic, since it would resume from there rather than from the start. After that, I'd sanity-check the topic name itself for an exact match — a one-character typo subscribing to the wrong topic is an easy, very common mistake. Once I've ruled those out, I'd produce a brand-new test message while watching the consumer live, which is the clearest way to confirm the pipeline actually works end to end.
commonMistakes: Not realizing auto.offset.reset = 'latest' means a new consumer skips everything already in the topic
Assuming the consumer is broken instead of checking the topic name for an exact-match typo
Not checking whether the consumer group already has committed offsets from an earlier, different test run
Testing only against historical messages instead of producing a fresh message to confirm the pipeline live
keyPoints: auto.offset.reset ('earliest' vs. 'latest') controls whether a new consumer sees historical messages
Consumer groups resume from their last committed offset, not necessarily the beginning
Topic name must match exactly, case-sensitively
Producing a fresh test message is the clearest way to confirm the pipeline end to end

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies auto.offset.reset / consumer group offset as the likely cause
Describes how to confirm it
Mentions a topic name mismatch as a secondary cause

questions.title: Queries against a Delta table have gotten slow due to too many small files
questions.prompt: A Delta table that receives frequent small append writes throughout the day has gradually gotten much slower to query, even though the total amount of data hasn't grown dramatically. What's the likely cause, and what command addresses it?
questions.modelAnswer: Frequent small appends each write their own small Parquet file underneath the Delta table, and over time this produces the 'small file problem' -- instead of a reasonable number of appropriately-sized files, the table ends up backed by thousands of tiny ones. Reading the table means opening and reading from every one of those files, and the per-file overhead (opening, reading metadata/footer, closing) starts to dominate query time even though the actual data volume is the same. The fix is running OPTIMIZE on the table, which compacts many small files into a smaller number of appropriately-sized ones (optionally combined with ZORDER BY on a frequently-filtered column to colocate related data within those files), directly addressing the file-count problem without changing the data itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to throw more compute at this — it's worth checking file count and size before assuming the cluster needs to be bigger. Frequent small appends are a classic way to end up with the small file problem: every little write creates its own small Parquet file, and eventually the table is backed by far more files than it needs, so just opening and closing each one starts to dominate query time even though the data itself hasn't grown much. Running OPTIMIZE on the table compacts those small files into a sensible number of larger ones, and if there's a column that's frequently filtered on, I'd pair it with ZORDER BY that column to colocate related data within the compacted files too. I'd also make sure I'm not confusing this with VACUUM, which removes old unreferenced files rather than compacting current ones — they solve two different problems.
commonMistakes: Assuming slow queries always mean more compute/cluster size is needed, rather than checking file count/size first
Not running OPTIMIZE periodically on tables with frequent small writes
Confusing OPTIMIZE (compacts files) with VACUUM (removes old, unreferenced files) -- they solve different problems
Running OPTIMIZE once and assuming the small-file problem is permanently solved, rather than scheduling it to run periodically
keyPoints: Frequent small appends create many small underlying files (the small file problem)
Per-file overhead dominates query time once file count grows large
OPTIMIZE compacts small files into larger ones
ZORDER can be combined with OPTIMIZE for frequently-filtered columns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the small-file problem
Proposes OPTIMIZE as the fix
Distinguishes OPTIMIZE from VACUUM

questions.title: Auto Loader isn't picking up files that just landed
questions.prompt: An Auto Loader stream has been reliably loading new CSV files into a bronze table for days. An hour ago, a fresh batch of files landed in the source folder, but they still haven't shown up in the target table. The stream shows no errors. What are the most likely explanations, and what would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: The first and most likely explanation isn't anything about the files at all -- it's that the stream simply isn't running right now. A streaming read only picks up new files while its writeStream query is actively executing (or, if triggered with availableNow/once on a schedule, only at the moment it last ran), so the first check is confirming the job or cluster running this stream is actually active, not idle, failed-and-stopped, or waiting on its next scheduled trigger. If the stream genuinely is running, the next check is the checkpoint and schema location -- if those paths were pointed at a different folder by mistake, or the checkpoint is from an entirely different source, Auto Loader would be faithfully tracking progress against the wrong thing and never see the new files land in the real source folder. Only after confirming the stream is live and pointed at the correct checkpoint/source would it make sense to dig into discovery-mode-specific causes, such as a notification-based setup where the underlying cloud event queue has a backlog or misconfiguration.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd suspect anything exotic, I'd check the boring thing first: is this stream actually running right now, or did the job finish, fail, or just not get triggered yet on its schedule? A structured streaming source like Auto Loader only discovers new files while it's actively executing, so a stream that's sitting idle or crashed silently looks exactly like 'files aren't showing up,' even though nothing is actually wrong with Auto Loader itself. If it is running, my next check is the checkpoint and schema location paths -- if those got pointed at the wrong folder by copy-paste, the stream is faithfully doing its job against a different source than the one I think it's watching. I'd only start looking at something like a notification-queue backlog, which is specific to notification mode, after I've ruled out the two much more common causes first.
commonMistakes: Assuming something is wrong with Auto Loader's file-tracking logic before checking whether the stream is even currently running
Not verifying the checkpointLocation and schemaLocation actually point at the intended source folder
Jumping straight to an exotic notification-queue explanation before ruling out the stream simply being idle or stopped
Restarting the stream with a fresh checkpoint as a first troubleshooting step, which can cause files to be reprocessed or skipped unintentionally
keyPoints: A streaming source only discovers new files while actively running -- check job/cluster status first
Verify checkpointLocation and schemaLocation point at the actual intended source, not a leftover or mistaken path
Rule out the stream simply being idle before suspecting a deeper Auto Loader or notification-queue issue
Avoid resetting the checkpoint as a first troubleshooting step, since that can skip or reprocess files

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies checking whether the stream is actually running as the first step
Correctly identifies checkpoint/schema location misconfiguration as a likely cause
Appropriately sequences troubleshooting from common to exotic causes

questions.title: Why Dev, QA, and Production stay separate
questions.prompt: Why does a BI team typically maintain separate Dev, QA, and Production SQL Server environments, and promote a change through them in that fixed order, instead of just building and testing directly against the Production database that live reports and real users already depend on?
questions.modelAnswer: Dev is where new work is actually built, and it's expected to be unstable -- half-finished packages, broken queries, and throwaway test data are all normal there, and critically, none of that instability is visible to anyone who depends on real numbers. QA is a separate, more stable environment with data that resembles Production, used specifically to verify a change behaves correctly before any real user is ever exposed to it -- this is where testing is supposed to happen, not in Dev and not in Production. Production is the environment real business users and live reports actually run against, and it's deliberately the last environment any change reaches, only after being built in Dev and then validated in QA. Testing directly against Production is risky for two concrete reasons: an in-progress or buggy change can lock, corrupt, or simply show wrong numbers in data that live reports depend on right now, and there's no safe way to test something genuinely risky -- a schema change, a large bulk load -- without potentially causing a real outage if it goes wrong. Promoting a change through Dev, then QA, then Production in that fixed order guarantees every change gets at least one chance to fail somewhere that doesn't matter yet before it ever reaches somewhere that does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what's allowed to break where. Dev is allowed to break -- that's the whole point of it, it's where I'm actively building and nobody real is looking at it. QA is where I prove a change actually works against data that looks like the real thing, before any real user sees it. Production is the one environment where breaking something has an actual business cost, so it's deliberately the last stop, not the first. If I skipped straight to testing in Production, the two real risks are: a change that's still buggy could corrupt or lock data that a live report is reading from right now, and there's no safe way to rehearse something genuinely risky, like a schema change, without actually risking the outage I was trying to avoid. The fixed Dev-then-QA-then-Production order is really just making sure every change gets tested somewhere low-stakes before it reaches somewhere high-stakes.
commonMistakes: Making a direct change in Production 'just this once' to save time
Treating QA as optional for a change that 'seems small' instead of validating it there first
Letting QA's data drift so far from Production's that it stops catching real issues
Conflating Dev and QA as the same environment instead of recognizing their different purposes (building vs. validating)
keyPoints: Dev is for building and is expected to be unstable, isolated from real users
QA validates a change against production-like data before any real user is exposed to it
Production is the last environment reached, only after Dev and QA
Direct Production changes risk live data and can't safely rehearse risky operations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the purpose of each environment (Dev, QA, Production)
Correctly explains the risk of testing directly in Production
Explains why the promotion order matters

questions.title: Why orchestrate with Airflow instead of a cron job or Task Scheduler
questions.prompt: A pipeline currently runs as a Windows Task Scheduler job that kicks off a script once a night. Why would you recommend moving that to Airflow once the pipeline grows to several dependent steps, instead of just adding more scheduled scripts?
questions.modelAnswer: A scheduler like Task Scheduler or cron is good at exactly one thing: triggering a script at a fixed time. It has no concept of a dependency between two separate scheduled jobs -- if job B needs job A to finish first, the only way to enforce that with plain scheduling is guessing a safe time gap between them and hoping job A always finishes within that window, which becomes fragile and eventually wrong as job A's runtime varies. It also has no built-in retry logic for a single failed step, no visibility into which specific step failed versus which succeeded, and no easy way to re-run just the one step that failed without re-running everything. Airflow's DAG model replaces guessed time gaps with explicit dependencies (A must actually complete before B starts, regardless of how long A took), gives each task its own retry policy, and provides a UI showing exactly which task succeeded, failed, or is still running, plus the ability to re-run just one failed task without re-triggering the whole pipeline. The point where this switch becomes worth it is specifically when a pipeline grows multiple genuinely dependent steps -- a single standalone nightly script has little reason to move to Airflow at all; the value appears once ordering, retries, and partial-failure visibility actually start to matter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say the core issue with chaining Task Scheduler jobs is that there's no real dependency between them -- just a guessed time gap. If job A usually takes 20 minutes, I'd schedule job B to start 30 minutes later and hope that's always enough of a buffer, but the day job A runs long, job B starts against incomplete data with nothing catching that. Airflow replaces that guess with an actual dependency: B simply doesn't start until A has genuinely finished successfully, no matter how long A took. I'd also point out the visibility difference -- when something fails at 2 AM, Task Scheduler gives me very little to go on, while Airflow's UI shows me exactly which task in the chain failed, lets me retry just that one task, and can alert me automatically. I wouldn't necessarily move a single standalone script to Airflow just because it's nightly -- the real trigger for making this move is once there are genuinely multiple dependent steps where getting the order and retries right actually starts to matter.
commonMistakes: Scheduling dependent jobs with guessed time gaps instead of enforcing a real completion-based dependency
Not recognizing the retry and partial-failure-visibility gap in a plain scheduler compared to Airflow
Recommending Airflow for a single standalone script that has no actual dependencies to manage
Assuming the migration is purely about scheduling syntax rather than dependency enforcement and observability
keyPoints: A plain scheduler (cron/Task Scheduler) has no concept of a dependency between separate jobs, only guessed time gaps
Airflow enforces real completion-based dependencies between tasks, regardless of how long any one task took
Airflow provides retry logic, per-task status visibility, and the ability to re-run just one failed task
The move is worth it once a pipeline has multiple genuinely dependent steps, not for a single standalone script

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the dependency-enforcement gap in a plain scheduler
Correctly identifies the retry/visibility advantages of Airflow
Correctly scopes when this move is actually worth making

questions.title: Why keep raw data in the bronze layer instead of cleaning it immediately
questions.prompt: In a medallion (bronze/silver/gold) architecture, why deliberately land data into the bronze layer completely raw and unchanged, instead of cleaning and transforming it on the way in to save a step?
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze is a verbatim, untouched copy of exactly what the source sent, kept specifically so there's always a reliable point to reprocess from. If a downstream transformation turns out to have a bug, or a business rule changes months later, having the original raw data still sitting in bronze means reprocessing can start over from the true source again -- if the raw data had been transformed immediately and the original discarded, a bug discovered later could be unrecoverable, because the only copy left is the one built from flawed logic. Silver takes bronze and applies cleaning, deduplication, and conforming to a defined schema; gold aggregates silver into business-ready, consumption-ready tables. Separating these stages also isolates failures: a broken silver transformation doesn't corrupt bronze, and a mistake can be fixed by just rerunning silver against the bronze data that's still safely sitting there untouched.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as an insurance policy, not an extra step for its own sake. Bronze is deliberately a verbatim copy of exactly what the source sent — nothing cleaned, nothing reshaped — specifically so there's always a true, unaltered starting point to go back to. If a bug is found in a silver transformation six months later, or a business rule changes and historical numbers need to be recomputed under the new rule, I can rerun silver against that original bronze data and get it right, because the raw truth never left. If I'd transformed on the way in and thrown away the original, that fix might not even be possible — the only copy I'd have left is the one built from the flawed logic. Keeping the stages separate also means a broken silver job doesn't put bronze at risk at all; I can fix silver and just rerun it.
commonMistakes: Transforming data on ingestion and discarding the raw original, losing the ability to reprocess from the true source later
Treating bronze/silver/gold as just three copies of the same thing
Not reprocessing from bronze after fixing a transformation bug, instead patching only the downstream table and leaving history inconsistent
Skipping the bronze layer entirely to save storage, not realizing what's given up by doing so
keyPoints: Bronze = raw, untouched copy of the source, kept for reprocessing
Silver = cleaned/conformed; gold = business-ready aggregates
Keeping raw data preserves the ability to recover from a downstream bug or a later rule change
Separating stages isolates failures -- a broken silver job doesn't corrupt bronze

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why bronze stays raw/untouched
Correctly describes the roles of silver and gold

questions.title: Why Kafka's publish-subscribe model decouples producers from consumers
questions.prompt: Architecturally, why does routing data through a Kafka topic -- rather than having a source system call a destination system's API directly -- decouple producers from consumers, and why does that decoupling matter?
questions.modelAnswer: In a direct point-to-point integration, the source system has to know who its consumers are, call each one directly, and deal with a consumer being slow, down, or needing to be added later -- every new consumer means a code change on the producer side. With Kafka, a producer only knows about the topic it writes to, with no knowledge of who, if anyone, is reading it; any number of independent consumers (or consumer groups) can read that same topic at their own pace, including ones added long after the producer was written, without the producer ever being modified. This decoupling means producers and consumers can be developed, deployed, scaled, and can fail independently of each other -- a consumer being temporarily down doesn't block the producer from continuing to publish, because Kafka retains the messages in the topic for the consumer to catch up on later, within its retention window.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd contrast it directly with a direct API call. If a source system calls a destination's API directly, it has to know that destination exists, handle it being slow or down, and get a code change whenever a new downstream consumer needs the same data. With Kafka, the producer just writes to its topic and is done — it has no idea who's reading it, and it doesn't need to. Any number of consumers, including ones written and deployed long after the producer, can read that same topic independently, at their own pace. The practical benefit I care about most is failure isolation: if a consumer goes down for an hour, the producer keeps publishing without any disruption, because Kafka holds onto those messages in the topic until the consumer comes back and catches up, within whatever retention window is configured.

Not realizing a slow or down consumer doesn't block the producer, since Kafka buffers messages in the topic
Thinking adding a new consumer requires any change to the producer's code at all
Treating Kafka as functionally identical to a direct point-to-point integration with extra steps, rather than a genuinely decoupled model

Any number of independent consumers can read the same topic at their own pace
A down/slow consumer doesn't block the producer, since messages are retained

questions.title: Unity Catalog's three-level namespace
questions.prompt: What is Unity Catalog's three-level namespace (catalog.schema.table) in Databricks, and why does organizing data that way matter once more than one team shares a workspace?
questions.modelAnswer: Unity Catalog adds a top level -- catalog -- above the familiar schema.table structure, giving every table a fully-qualified three-part name: catalog.schema.table. The catalog level typically separates data by environment or business domain (for example a dev catalog and a prod catalog, or separate catalogs per business unit), the schema level groups related tables within that catalog, and table is the familiar individual table. This matters once multiple teams share one workspace because without that top catalog level, every schema and table name has to be unique across the entire workspace, which doesn't scale -- two different teams can't both have a 'sales' schema with a 'customers' table. With catalogs, 'analytics_catalog.sales.customers' and 'marketing_catalog.sales.customers' can coexist cleanly, and permissions (grants) can be applied at any of the three levels, so an entire catalog can be locked down to one team without having to grant or deny access table by table.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as schema.table getting a layer added on top of it. Catalog typically separates things by environment or business domain — a dev catalog, a prod catalog, maybe one catalog per business unit — and schema and table work underneath it the way they always did. The reason this actually matters once a workspace has more than one team in it is naming collisions: without a catalog level, two teams can't both have a 'sales' schema with a 'customers' table, because the names have to be unique across the whole workspace. With catalogs, 'analytics_catalog.sales.customers' and 'marketing_catalog.sales.customers' can both exist without conflict. The other thing I'd highlight is that permissions aren't just table-by-table — I can grant or revoke access at the catalog level and lock down an entire team's catalog in one move, rather than managing access on every individual table underneath it.

questions.title: Managed vs. external Delta tables
questions.prompt: In Unity Catalog, when would you deliberately choose an external Delta table over a managed one, architecturally, and what do you give up by doing so?
questions.modelAnswer: A managed table's underlying data files live inside storage that Unity Catalog fully owns and controls -- dropping the table deletes the actual data files along with the catalog entry, and there's no separate location to manage. An external table instead points at a storage location the data genuinely lives in independently of Unity Catalog (an existing ADLS Gen2 path, for example), registering an external location and credential so Unity Catalog can govern access to it -- but dropping an external table only removes the catalog entry, not the underlying files, which remain exactly where they were. The architectural case for external tables is when the data must continue to exist and be reachable outside Unity Catalog's management -- shared with another tool or team that reads those same files directly, or data that was already sitting in a specific location before Unity Catalog existed and can't simply be moved. What's given up by choosing external is some of the simplicity of managed tables: the storage location and lifecycle have to be tracked and administered separately, and a careless drop doesn't clean up storage the way a managed table's drop does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame the choice around one question: does this data need to keep existing and be reachable independent of Unity Catalog? If the answer is no -- this table's lifecycle should be fully owned and cleaned up by Unity Catalog -- I'd default to managed, since dropping it correctly removes both the catalog entry and the actual files, with nothing left to manually clean up. If the answer is yes -- another tool or team reads those same files directly, or the data already lives in a specific ADLS location that can't be moved -- I'd register it as external, pointing Unity Catalog at that existing location through an external location and credential. What I'd be honest about giving up with external tables is some of that automatic lifecycle management: I now own tracking where the files actually live and making sure a drop doesn't leave me thinking data is gone when it's actually still sitting there, or vice versa.
commonMistakes: Assuming dropping an external table deletes the underlying files the same way a managed table drop does
Defaulting to external tables everywhere out of habit, losing the lifecycle simplicity managed tables provide
Not registering an external location/credential properly, leading to Unity Catalog being unable to govern access to the external path
Treating the managed/external choice as cosmetic rather than a real decision about data ownership and lifecycle
keyPoints: Managed tables: Unity Catalog owns the storage; dropping the table deletes the actual data files
External tables: data lives in a separate location Unity Catalog governs but doesn't own; dropping only removes the catalog entry
Choose external when data must remain reachable independent of Unity Catalog's lifecycle
External tables trade away some automatic lifecycle simplicity for that independence

questions.title: Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines vs. plain notebooks
questions.prompt: Architecturally, what does Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines add over writing the same bronze-to-silver-to-gold transformations as a sequence of plain notebook cells run in order?
questions.modelAnswer: A plain notebook pipeline is imperative -- each cell explicitly tells Spark what to do, in the exact order written, and the notebook itself has no built-in concept of the dependency graph between the tables it's building beyond that cell order, nor any built-in way to validate data quality as it flows through. Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines takes a declarative approach instead: you describe each table (bronze, silver, gold) as its own definition, and the dependency graph between them is inferred automatically from which tables reference which, rather than being manually sequenced cell by cell. On top of that, it adds expectations -- declarative data-quality rules attached directly to a table definition, which can drop, flag, or fail rows that violate them -- something a plain notebook would have to implement by hand with ad hoc filtering and logging. The practical result is that Lakeflow handles orchestration and quality enforcement as first-class, declared concerns, while a plain notebook pipeline leaves both as something the author has to build and maintain themselves.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the plain-notebook approach as imperative -- I'm the one writing, in order, exactly what happens to the data at each step, and if I get the cell order wrong, nothing catches that for me. Lakeflow flips that around: I describe each table I want -- bronze, silver, gold -- as its own definition, and it figures out the dependency graph between them on its own, based on what each one actually reads from. The other piece I'd specifically call out is expectations -- I can declare a data-quality rule right on a table definition, saying what should happen to a row that violates it, instead of writing my own ad hoc filtering and logging to catch bad rows in a notebook. The real shift is that orchestration and data quality become things I declare rather than things I have to hand-build and maintain myself.

Assuming the dependency graph still has to be manually sequenced, rather than inferred from table references
Not knowing expectations are a built-in, declared mechanism rather than something hand-coded
Describing the difference only in terms of syntax rather than the underlying imperative-vs-declarative shift

Lakeflow is declarative -- each table is defined, and dependencies are inferred automatically

Lakeflow turns orchestration and quality into declared concerns instead of hand-built ones

questions.title: Job clusters vs. all-purpose clusters
questions.prompt: Architecturally, why would you run a scheduled, unattended pipeline on a job cluster rather than an all-purpose cluster, and why does that choice matter for cost?
questions.modelAnswer: An all-purpose cluster is meant to stay running and be shared -- multiple people attach notebooks to it interactively throughout the day, and it keeps running (and billing) between those sessions unless manually or automatically terminated after idle time. A job cluster is created fresh specifically for one scheduled job run, and is automatically terminated the moment that run finishes, rather than idling afterward waiting for the next person to use it. Running a scheduled, unattended pipeline on an all-purpose cluster means paying for that cluster to sit running between scheduled runs (or relying on an idle-termination setting that might not line up cleanly with the schedule), whereas a job cluster is only ever billed for the exact duration of that one run, with nothing left idling afterward. The architectural reason to default scheduled jobs to job clusters isn't just cost, though cost is the most visible benefit -- it's also isolation: a job cluster's configuration is dedicated to that one job and isn't affected by someone else's interactive notebook work consuming resources on a shared all-purpose cluster at the same time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame all-purpose clusters as the shared, always-on workspace multiple people attach to during the day, versus job clusters as something spun up fresh for exactly one scheduled run and torn down the second that run finishes. If I ran a nightly pipeline on an all-purpose cluster, I'm either paying for it to sit running between runs, or depending on an idle-termination setting that might not line up with my actual schedule. A job cluster only ever costs money for the exact minutes that one run actually took. Cost is the benefit everyone notices first, but I'd also point out isolation -- a job cluster's resources are dedicated to that one job, so it's not competing with someone else's interactive notebook work on a shared cluster at the same time, which matters for predictable run times just as much as it matters for the bill.
commonMistakes: Running every scheduled, unattended job on a shared all-purpose cluster by default
Assuming idle-termination on an all-purpose cluster makes it equivalent to a job cluster's cost profile
Thinking the difference is purely about cost and missing the resource-isolation benefit
Using a job cluster for genuinely interactive, exploratory work where an all-purpose cluster is actually the right fit

Job clusters are created for one scheduled run and automatically terminate when it finishes
Job clusters avoid paying for idle time between scheduled runs
Job clusters also isolate a scheduled job's resources from unrelated interactive work

questions.title: What Delta Sharing solves
questions.prompt: Architecturally, what problem does Delta Sharing solve for sharing data with a partner organization, compared to the two more obvious alternatives: exporting and emailing a file, or giving the partner direct database credentials?
questions.modelAnswer: Exporting and emailing a file produces an immediately stale, disconnected copy -- the moment the source data changes, the exported file is wrong, and there's no way to revoke it once it's been sent. Giving a partner direct database credentials solves the staleness problem but creates a much bigger one: the partner now has broad, standing access to systems and data far beyond what they actually need, with no fine-grained way to scope exactly which table or rows they can see, and revoking that access typically means a disruptive credential rotation. Delta Sharing is a third option built specifically for this case: it lets an organization share a live, governed view of specific tables with an external recipient, without copying the data and without handing over broad database credentials -- the recipient reads the current data directly (through a share), access is scoped to exactly what was shared, and it can be revoked at any time without affecting any other access the organization has granted. It solves the core tension between the other two options: staying current (like direct credentials) while staying narrowly scoped and revocable (like a controlled export, but without the staleness).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why the two obvious options both fall short. Emailing an exported file is simple, but it's a snapshot -- the second the real data changes, what I sent is wrong, and I have no way to pull it back once it's out. Handing over direct database credentials fixes the staleness problem, but now the partner has broad access to whatever that login can reach, with no easy way to say 'just this one table, nothing else,' and revoking it usually means rotating a credential that might be used for other things too. Delta Sharing is built to avoid both problems: I share a specific table as a live, read-only view, the partner always sees current data without me copying anything, and the access is scoped to exactly what I shared and revocable on its own, without touching any other credentials or access I've granted elsewhere.

questions.title: What Photon is, at a glance
questions.prompt: What is Photon in Databricks, at a basic level, and why doesn't turning it on require rewriting any of your existing Spark code?
questions.modelAnswer: Photon is a native, vectorized query engine Databricks built to execute Spark workloads faster than the standard JVM-based Spark execution engine, particularly for SQL and DataFrame operations -- scans, joins, aggregations. It sits underneath the same Spark APIs a developer already writes against, as an alternative execution engine for the same logical plan, rather than a different API or language developers have to learn and rewrite their code into. Because of that, turning Photon on for a cluster doesn't require touching existing PySpark or Spark SQL code at all -- the DataFrame/SQL code describes what to compute, and Photon (when enabled) is simply a faster implementation handling how that computation is physically executed under the hood, invisible to the code itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe Photon as a faster engine running underneath the exact same code I already write, not a new thing I have to learn. My DataFrame or Spark SQL code describes what I want computed, and that description doesn't change at all whether Photon is on or off -- what changes is how that computation actually gets executed physically, with Photon's native, vectorized execution typically outperforming the standard engine, especially on SQL-heavy workloads like scans, joins, and aggregations. That separation between 'what to compute' and 'how it's executed' is exactly why turning Photon on for a cluster is a configuration choice, not a rewrite -- the same notebook that ran before Photon was enabled keeps working identically after, just faster on the operations Photon accelerates.

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new BI team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. A junior new hire should resist the urge to over-explain or justify slow progress at length -- stand-up is meant to be short, and a longer conversation about a specific blocker belongs in a follow-up afterward, not consuming the whole meeting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the Lookup for the Customer dimension and started on the fact table load. Today I'm wiring up the error output so bad rows get redirected instead of failing the whole package. I'm blocked on getting read access to the QA staging database, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real ticket instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.

Being vague ('still working on it') instead of naming the specific ticket or task
Saving a blocker until later instead of surfacing it the moment it's identified
Turning stand-up into a long problem-solving discussion instead of flagging it briefly and following up afterward

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. I'd flag it the moment I realize it, specifically naming what I actually need to get unblocked, rather than just saying 'I'm stuck,' because a specific ask is what actually gets someone to act on it quickly.

questions.title: Explaining why the team works in sprints, not all at once
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team can't just build the whole report and show it to them when it's completely done, instead of working in two-week sprints. How would you explain the difference between Agile and Waterfall to them, and why your team works the way it does?
questions.modelAnswer: Waterfall fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and fully understood up front, moving through fixed phases once in order -- but if a requirement turns out to be wrong, that's usually not discovered until most of the work is already built, which makes it expensive to fix at that point. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating two-week cycles, each one producing something real and working that the stakeholder can actually see and react to. The explanation should connect directly to the stakeholder's own interest rather than staying abstract: working in sprints means they get to say 'that's not quite what I meant' after two weeks of effort instead of after two months, which protects them, not just the team. It's also worth clarifying that a sprint still produces a genuinely working, shippable piece of the report each cycle -- not an unfinished fragment -- so showing it early isn't showing something broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip straight to what's in it for them. If we built the whole thing in one long pass and only showed it at the end, and it turned out we misunderstood something on day one, we wouldn't find that out until the entire report was already built -- which is expensive and slow to fix at that point. Working in two-week sprints means every two weeks you get to look at something real and tell us if we're headed the wrong direction, while that's still cheap to correct. I'd also be clear that what you're seeing every two weeks isn't a half-finished mess -- it's a genuinely working slice of the report, just not the whole thing yet. That's really the whole point of sprints: catching a misunderstanding in week two instead of week eight.

questions.title: Communicating during a live production incident
questions.prompt: Two days after a dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region all month. Walk me through how you'd investigate, and what you would communicate to the manager while you're still figuring out the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the two parts of this question clearly. On investigation: start with the simplest explanation before anything complex -- did the dashboard's scheduled refresh actually run last night at all -- then work backward from the visible symptom toward the source, checking whether the ETL load completed for that region, whether the issue is in the underlying data or just a report-level filter, rather than guessing at a cause. On communication: send an honest, specific acknowledgment quickly -- confirming the report was received, that it's being looked into, and giving a concrete time to expect an update -- rather than staying silent until a fix is confirmed. It's expected and professional to communicate while still investigating, not only once the cause is found; silence during that window reads as neglect even when real work is happening behind the scenes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into what I say and what I actually do, and do the communication part first. Within a few minutes I'd send something like: 'Thanks for flagging this -- I'm looking into it now and will have an update for you by end of day.' That costs me almost nothing and tells the manager they haven't been forgotten. Then I'd investigate from the simplest explanation outward: did last night's scheduled refresh actually complete, or did it fail silently? If the refresh ran fine, I'd check whether that region's rows actually loaded into the fact table for this month, or whether this is a filter or slicer issue purely inside the report itself. I'd keep narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source rather than guessing at something exotic first. Once I actually find the cause, I'd follow up with a clear explanation of what happened and what I changed -- not just a silent fix with no note at all.

questions.title: Turning a vague business request into a user story
questions.prompt: A sales director emails you: 'Our regional managers keep asking me for last month's numbers by email. I need a dashboard that shows revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically, so they can check it themselves.' How would you turn that into a proper user story with acceptance criteria before you start building anything?
questions.modelAnswer: A user story is written from the user's point of view, in the shape 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' -- for this request: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' A story alone is too vague to know when it's actually done, which is what acceptance criteria are for -- specific, checkable conditions, such as 'the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning, with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's assigned territory.' Just as important is noticing what the original email left out: it never says what should happen when a region has zero sales for the month. A strong answer explicitly surfaces that gap -- either asking the sales director directly, or documenting a reasonable judgment call as its own acceptance criterion -- rather than silently guessing and discovering the wrong assumption after the dashboard is already built.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building from that email directly -- I'd turn it into a story first: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' Then I'd write acceptance criteria that are actually checkable, not just a vague sense of done -- something like 'reflects yesterday's closed sales by 7 AM with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's own territory.' The thing I'd specifically flag before writing a single line of DAX is that the email never says what should happen if a region had zero sales that month -- show it as zero, blank, or leave it off the list entirely? I'd either ask the sales director directly or write down my own reasonable assumption as an explicit acceptance criterion, because guessing silently on that detail is exactly the kind of thing that comes back wrong during UAT.
